 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §     PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                    §              OF TEXAS


                            AEP COMPANIES’ COMMENTS
                    ON COMMISSION'S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

        AEP Texas Inc. (a wholly owned subsidiary of American Electric Power Inc. (AEP)) and

Electric Transmission Texas, LLC (a joint venture between AEP and Berkshire Hathaway Energy)

(collectively, the AEP Companies) provide these comments in response to the Commission’s

March 12, 2026, Proposal for Publication (PFP) regarding large load interconnection standards

under PURA § 37.0561. The AEP Companies include a redline version of the PFP as Attachment

A.


                                  I.    GENERAL COMMENTS

        The AEP Companies support language in the Commission’s implementation of SB6 that

maintains the existing construct of treating network upgrades as system assets and recovering their

costs broadly through Transmission Cost of Service given the system-wide benefits that they

provide, but requires a contribution in aid of construction (CIAC) for direct connect facilities.

Charging large load customers a set fee per MW that is not tied to actual costs is not the best way

to ensure that customers causing the costs are made responsible for those costs. Ensuring that the

customers causing these broader investments in the transmission system are responsible for paying

their fair share of the costs may require adjustment to the allocation across the classes to capture

the intent of SB6. The rate design construct should ensure that other rate classes are protected

from costs caused by the growth in large loads . In particular, using a demand charge as part of a

 large load tariff1 construct may better achieve the intent of SB6 than the language proposed in

subsection (f)(7) that would require utilities to offset rate costs by charging a non-refundable

$50,000/MW fee and (g)(4) regarding retention of security if a large load reduces its requested

size.


                    II.   COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION



        Section (d) and (f): Commission-approved pro forma for the intermediate and

interconnection agreement

        The AEP Companies support requiring both the intermediate agreement and the

interconnection agreement to be based on Commission-approved pro forma agreements and

removal of the requirement that an interconnection agreement will be executed not later than 30

days after completion of the interconnection studies. The ERCOT batch process will support a

natural timeline for intermediate agreements to be executed prior to the inclusion in a batch and

interconnection agreements to be executed in the window between when the initial study is

completed and prior to the initiation of the batch refinement period. Use of pro forma agreements

could help ensure execution to occurs within that window by limiting negotiations of project-

specific deviations, rather than reopening standardized terms. Requiring pro forma agreements

supports the Commission’s and stakeholders’ shared objective of consistency and alignment across

utilities, would streamline implementation of the Commission’s standards, and ensure that

similarly situated large load customers are subject to uniform terms.

 Section (c)(10): Requested peak demand definition

        The Commission should provide additional guidance on the definition of requested peak

demand to ensure consistent input into ERCOT protocols for the batch study process. Specifically,

clarification is needed regarding whether requested peak demand is intended to be inclusive of

behind-the-meter load and how peak demand should be determined for self-limiting loads.

        The AEP Companies support a definition that sets the requested peak demand at the total

gross demand the large load customer can draw from the system. This definition would reflect the

maximum demand that the large load customer could reasonably place on the ERCOT system and

the current process for how behind-the-meter loads are required to be studied.



Sections (d)(4) and (f)(4): Attestation that customer meets the requirements as set forth in

§25.194 of this Title

        Both sections (d)(4) and (f)(4) require an attestation from the customer that it has the

necessary approvals from state and local regulatory authorities. The AEP Companies suggest

expanding this attestation to require the customer to attest that the large load customer meets the

requirements of § 25.194 to ensure that the large load customer acknowledges and accepts their

obligations under the Commission’s large load interconnection standards.



Section (d)(6): Backup generating facilities

        The AEP Companies recommend striking the reference to the “interconnecting TSP”

because, where the DSP and TSP are separate entities, the DSP is the entity providing certificated

retail delivery service. Accordingly, the information at issue is relevant only to the DSP and is not

necessary for the TSP. Additionally, the large load customer should notify the interconnecting


Project No. 58481                                                           AEP Companies’ Comments
                                                 3
 DSP if its plans for backup generating facilities materially changes as this information is needed

to meet its obligations as the transmission operator of the load.



Section (d)(7): Power Supply

         Large load development timelines and on‑site generation strategies often evolve as

projects move from concept through construction and in-service. Currently, a large load customer

is required to notify the TSP of material changes to its plans for on‑site generation. AEP requests

that the Commission consider that there are circumstances where the on-site generation material

change could promote better system‑wide outcomes, operational coordination, and reliability.

Under those circumstances, at this stage in the process, a large load customer should be permitted

to change its study parameters and maintain the ability to proceed through the process.



Section (d)(9): Study fee

        AEP Companies suggest removing the interconnecting TSP as one of the entities collecting

the study fee. The interconnecting DSP should collect the interconnection study fee because the

DSP maintains the direct relationship with the large load customer and serves as the primary point

of contact throughout the interconnection process. Centralizing study fee collection with the DSP

provides a single, clear interface for the customer, reduces administrative complexity, and supports

timely coordination with ERCOT and the interconnecting TSP within batch study deadlines.



Section (d)(10): Financial Security on a dollar per MW basis

        The inclusion of multi‑party agreements enables the DSP and TSP to hold a proportional

allocation of financial security that is commensurate with the risk and costs each entity is


Project No. 58481                                                          AEP Companies’ Comments
                                                  4
 responsible for incurring. The rule should specifically contemplate that each entity will hold its

proportional share of the total estimated costs associated with the interconnection.



Section (d)(10)(C)-(D), (11)(C)-(D), and (f)(10)(B): Credit rating and submission of financial

records

        The AEP Companies suggest revisions to the credit ratings requirements to clarify that the

credit rating requirement should be based on ratings issued by both Standard & Poor’s and

Moody’s, unless the large load customer is only rated by one agency. If an entity has a credit rating

from one of the agencies that is below the standard in the rule, the interconnecting DSP or TSP

should not be required to accept the corporate or parental guaranty or letter of credit. Additionally,

the customer should simply be required to provide proof of its credit ratings to demonstrate

financial stability. There is no need for a separate review of financial records or statements because

the financial evaluation contemplated by this requirement is already encompassed within the

applicable credit ratings of the customer or guarantor.



Section (e): Interconnection Study

        The PFP requires that 60 days after an intermediate agreement is executed, the

interconnecting DSP or TSP must coordinate with ERCOT to initiate an interconnection study.

The AEP Companies recommend that the timing of interconnection studies be dictated by the

ERCOT batch study process to avoid conflicting timelines. A potential option would be to establish

signing window for intermediate agreements (e.g., reoccurring prior to each batch initiation). This

would allow customers, TSPs, and DSPs to understand when an agreement must be executed.

 Section (f)(7): Non-Refundable Interconnection Fee

         The AEP Companies recommend removing the non-refundable interconnection fee and

instead require a minimum bill. AEP Companies’ proposal for a minimum bill is through a

minimum demand charge as described in the AEP Companies comments in Project No. 58484.2

        Non-refundable fees or other offsets to DSP/TSP rate base have the potential to create a

situation where the utility is required to reduce rate base and revenue requirement from non-large

load related transmission invested capital because the non-refundable fee is in excess of the costs

to interconnect large load facilities. This results from the fact that set interconnection costs are not

linearly in proportion to the size of large load, and that if only “driveway costs” are incurred, the

required CIAC is already covering the costs created by the large load interconnection. This

construct would require transmission utilities to bear the risk associated with construction,

operation, and maintenance of the projects, while the associated reduction of rate base and revenue

requirement could negatively impact utilities’ credit ratings, ability to procure capital, and risk of

carrying only O&M for a growing proportion of new facilities built and owned by utilities.

        Additionally, if it remains, the proposal to include a non-refundable interconnection fee

would create ambiguity regarding the ability to draw down on financial security, which is typically

associated with an event of default. As currently drafted, the proposed definition also implies

enforcement mechanisms that are inconsistent with standard utility credit and security practices.

 Section (f)(8): Financial security for significant equipment or services

        The AEP Companies recommend removing section (f)(8) because it is unnecessary.

Section (9) states that a large load customer must pay all direct interconnection costs through a

CIAC, which includes long lead-time materials.



Sections (f)(9) and (10): CIAC and Financial Security for System Upgrades

        The AEP Companies recommend revisions to the rule language to clarify that CIAC for

“direct interconnection costs” is intended to address customer‑specific interconnection facilities

that are constructed solely to serve a large load customer and that would not otherwise be required

absent that customer’s request.

        Network upgrades that provide broader system benefits, such as maintaining system

reliability, relieving pre‑existing constraints, improving transfer capability, supporting multiple

customers, or accommodating regional load growth should not be treated as customer‑specific

facilities paid for through CIAC. Network upgrades that are triggered by a customer’s

interconnection request but ultimately serve to benefit the ERCOT system should have final cost

responsibility determined based on the identified scope of system benefits rather than solely on

causation. The financial security functions as an interim protection used during the interconnection

process prior to final cost allocation decisions, ensuring that customer‑caused upgrades are not

automatically assigned to a single customer when they provide broader system value.

        Additionally, AEP Companies recommend deletion of 25.194(f)(10)(C), regarding refund

of financial security because the language is an unnecessary restatement of other rule provisions

and potentially creates confusion with the proposed language in (f)(7), if that language is retained.




Project No. 58481                                                           AEP Companies’ Comments
                                                 7
 Additionally, it is in conflict with the ability of a utility to retain security as collateral in line with

a Large Load Tariff concept.

        Consistent with this approach, network upgrades should be addressed through a

transmission cost‑allocation methodology. The appropriate forum for resolving these issues is

Project No. 58484, where the Commission is considering transmission cost recovery and allocation

mechanisms on a broader, system‑wide basis. The AEP Companies propose a large load tariff

framework, as described in Section II. Large Load Tariff and in the comments in Project No.

58484, to address the cost allocation methodology for network upgrade costs. Such a framework

protects existing customers from stranded‑cost risk, reflects cost‑causation principles, and avoids

using CIAC or interconnection requirements to resolve broader cost‑allocation questions.


                                     III.    LARGE LOAD TARIFF



        The AEP Companies are generally supportive of Staff’s analysis of separate rate treatment

for large and flexible large loads3 and the inclusion of a minimum demand charge

recommendation, which has been adopted and is actively being considered in tariff structures and

contracts across many jurisdictions. Specifically, The AEP Companies propose that the

Commission consider the development of a large-load tariff similar to other states that includes:

(1) a minimum demand charge, (2) a minimum contract term, (3) clearly defined termination

charges to address stranded infrastructure costs, and (4) appropriate collateral or financial

assurance requirements. The AEP Companies describe this type of large-load tariff and its benefits

in more detail in Project No. 58484.

        The AEP Companies appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the PFP and the

Commission’s consideration of these comments in developing the final rule. An executive

summary of the comments is provided as the last page of this filing.

•   Sections (d) and (f): Both intermediate and interconnection agreements should be based on

    interconnection agreements should be removed, as the ERCOT batch process provides a
    natural execution window; pro forma agreements.
•   Section (c)(10): The Commission should provide additional guidance on the definition of
    requested peak demand to ensure consistent inputs into ERCOT’s batch study process,
    including clarification on behind‑the‑meter load and self‑limiting loads. The AEP Companies
    support defining requested peak demand as the maximum demand the large load customer is
    capable of drawing from the system.
•   Sections (d)(4) and (f)(4): The AEP Companies recommend expanding the required attestation
    to include a broad acknowledgment that the large load customer meets the requirements of
    §25.194, ensuring customers affirmatively acknowledge and accept their obligations under the
    Commission’s large load interconnection standards.

    TSP” because backup generation information is only relevant to the DSP providing certificated
    retail delivery service, and further recommend requiring customers to notify the
    interconnecting DSP of material changes to backup generation plans to support the DSP’s
    operational and planning obligations.
•   Section (d)(7): The AEP Companies recommend allowing large load customers to notify
    ERCOT of material changes to on-site generation plans and permitting updates to study
    parameters as projects evolve, improving planning accuracy and coordination while allowing
    projects to continue through the interconnection process.Section (d)(9): The AEP Companies
    suggest removing the interconnecting TSP as the entity collecting the study fee, as the DSP
    maintains the direct customer relationship, serves as the primary point of contact, reduces
    administrative complexity, and facilitates timely coordination with ERCOT and the TSP within
    batch study timelines.
•   Section (d)(10): The rule should contemplate that DSPs and TSPs may each hold a proportional
    share of financial security through multi-party agreements, reflecting the risks and costs each

                                  I.    GENERAL COMMENTS

        The AEP Companies support language in the Commission' s implementation of SB6 that

maintains the existing construct of treating network upgrades as system assets and recovering their

costs broadly through Transmission Cost of Service given the system-wide benefits that they

provide, but requires a contribution in aid of construction (CIAC) for direct connect facilities.

Charging large load customers a set fee per MW that is not tied to actual costs is not the best way

to ensure that customers causing the costs are made responsible for those costs. Ensuring that the

customers causing these broader investments in the transmission system are responsible for paying

their fair share of the costs may require adjustment to the allocation across the classes to capture

the intent of SB6. The rate design construct should ensure that other rate classes are protected

from costs caused by the growth in large loads . In particular, using a demand charge as part of a

                    II.   COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION



        Section (d) and (f): Commission-approved pro forma for the intermediate and

interconnection agreement

        The AEP Companies support requiring both the intermediate agreement and the

interconnection agreement to be based on Commission-approved pro forma agreements and

removal of the requirement that an interconnection agreement will be executed not later than 30

days after completion of the interconnection studies. The ERCOT batch process will support a

natural timeline for intermediate agreements to be executed prior to the inclusion in a batch and

interconnection agreements to be executed in the window between when the initial study is

completed and prior to the initiation of the batch refinement period. Use of pro forma agreements

could help ensure execution to occurs within that window by limiting negotiations of proj ect-

specific deviations, rather than reopening standardized terms. Requiring pro forma agreements

supports the Commission' s and stakeholders' shared objective of consistency and alignment across

utilities, would streamline implementation of the Commission' s standards, and ensure that

similarly situated large load customers are subject to uniform terms.

 Section (c)(10): Requested peak demand definition

        The Commission should provide additional guidance on the definition of requested peak

demand to ensure consistent input into ERCOT protocols for the batch study process. Specifically,

clarification is needed regarding whether requested peak demand is intended to be inclusive of

behind-the-meter load and how peak demand should be determined for self-limiting loads.

        The AEP Companies support a definition that sets the requested peak demand at the total

gross demand the large load customer can draw from the system. This definition would reflect the

maximum demand that the large load customer could reasonably place on the ERCOT system and

the current process for how behind-the-meter loads are required to be studied.



Sections (d)(4) and (f)(4): Attestation that customer meets the requirements as set forth in

§25.194 of this Title

        Both sections (d)(4) and (f)(4) require an attestation from the customer that it has the

necessary approvals from state and local regulatory authorities. The AEP Companies suggest

expanding this attestation to require the customer to attest that the large load customer meets the

requirements of § 25.194 to ensure that the large load customer acknowledges and accepts their

obligations under the Commission's large load interconnection standards.

Section (d)(7): Power Supply

         Large load development timelines and on-site generation strategies often evolve as

proj ects move from concept through construction and in-service. Currently, a large load customer

is required to notify the TSP of material changes to its plans for on-site generation. AEP requests

that the Commission consider that there are circumstances where the on-site generation material

change could promote better system-wide outcomes, operational coordination, and reliability.

Under those circumstances, at this stage in the process, a large load customer should be permitted

to change its study parameters and maintain the ability to proceed through the process.

        AEP Companies suggest removing the interconnecting TSP as one ofthe entities collecting

the study fee. The interconnecting DSP should collect the interconnection study fee because the

DSP maintains the direct relationship with the large load customer and serves as the primary point

of contact throughout the interconnection process. Centralizing study fee collection with the DSP

provides a single, clear interface for the customer, reduces administrative complexity, and supports

timely coordination with ERCOT and the interconnecting TSP within batch study deadlines.

        The AEP Companies suggest revisions to the credit ratings requirements to clarify that the

Section (e): Interconnection Study

        The PFP requires that 60 days after an intermediate agreement is executed, the

interconnecting DSP or TSP must coordinate with ERCOT to initiate an interconnection study.

The AEP Companies recommend that the timing of interconnection studies be dictated by the

ERCOT batch study process to avoid conflicting timelines. A potential option would be to establish

signing window for intermediate agreements (e.g., reoccurring prior to each batch initiation). This

would allow customers, TSPs, and DSPs to understand when an agreement must be executed.

 Section (f)(7): Non-Refundable Interconnection Fee

         The AEP Companies recommend removing the non-refundable interconnection fee and

instead require a minimum bill. AEP Companies' proposal for a minimum bill is through a

minimum demand charge as described in the AEP Companies comments in Project No. 58484.2

        Non-refundable fees or other offsets to DSP/TSP rate base have the potential to create a

situation where the utility is required to reduce rate base and revenue requirement from non-large

load related transmission invested capital because the non-refundable fee is in excess of the costs

to interconnect large load facilities. This results from the fact that set interconnection costs are not

linearly in proportion to the size of large load, and that if only "driveway costs" are incurred, the

required CIAC is already covering the costs created by the large load interconnection. This

construct would require transmission utilities to bear the risk associated with construction,

operation, and maintenance ofthe projects, while the associated reduction of rate base and revenue

requirement could negatively impact utilities' credit ratings, ability to procure capital, and risk of

carrying only 0&M for a growing proportion of new facilities built and owned by utilities.

        Additionally, if it remains, the proposal to include a non-refundable interconnection fee

would create ambiguity regarding the ability to draw down on financial security, which is typically

associated with an event of default. As currently drafted, the proposed definition also implies

enforcement mechanisms that are inconsistent with standard utility credit and security practices.

Sections (f)(9) and (10): CIAC and Financial Security for System Upgrades

        The AEP Companies recommend revisions to the rule language to clarify that CIAC for

"direct interconnection costs" is intended to address customer-specific interconnection facilities

that are constructed solely to serve a large load customer and that would not otherwise be required

absent that customer' s request.

        Network upgrades that provide broader system benefits, such as maintaining system

reliability, relieving pre-existing constraints, improving transfer capability, supporting multiple

customers, or accommodating regional load growth should not be treated as customer-specific

facilities paid for through CIAC. Network upgrades that are triggered by a customer' s

interconnection request but ultimately serve to benefit the ERCOT system should have final cost

responsibility determined based on the identified scope of system benefits rather than solely on

causation. The financial security functions as an interim protection used during the interconnection

process prior to final cost allocation decisions, ensuring that customer-caused upgrades are not

automatically assigned to a single customer when they provide broader system value.

        Additionally, AEP Companies recommend deletion of 25.194(f)(10)(C), regarding refund

of financial security because the language is an unnecessary restatement of other rule provisions

and potentially creates confusion with the proposed language in (f)(7), ifthat language is retained.

                                   III.    LARGE LOAD TARIFF



        The AEP Companies are generally supportive of Staff' s analysis of separate rate treatment

for large and flexible large loads3 and the inclusion of a minimum demand charge

recommendation, which has been adopted and is actively being considered in tariff structures and

contracts across many jurisdictions. Specifically, The AEP Companies propose that the

Commission consider the development of a large-load tariff similar to other states that includes:

(1) a minimum demand charge, (2) a minimum contract term, (3) clearly defined termination

charges to address stranded infrastructure costs, and (4) appropriate collateral or financial

assurance requirements. The AEP Companies describe this type of large-load tariff and its benefits

in more detail in Project No. 58484.
